title: Women
hookLine: the third order: marriage, divorce and vows
last: READ FROM THE PAGE; FAST TOWARD A CHANGE.

cards: The third order of the Mishnah has a one-word title: Nashim. Women. Open it expecting a book about women, and you'll find something else.
A tractate on what happens when a husband dies childless. One on the marriage contract. One on vows.
One on the nazirite, who promises to skip wine and let the hair grow. One on divorce, and one on how a marriage begins. What ties them together isn't a person.

teach.b: Nashim. Here's how the order works. First, it's about bonds you enter by your own words.
A marriage begins with an act and words of acceptance. A vow begins when you say it. A divorce ends with a document.
Each time, words create something real between two people.
The Torah, speaking of vows, says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth."
That verse could stand over the whole order. Second, why call it Women? Because the world it describes is one where a man usually acted and a woman was acted upon.

He gives the ring. He writes the divorce. The Torah's section on vows even goes on to discuss when a father or a husband may cancel a woman's vow; some readers say that's part of why vows sit here at all.
It's honest to say it plainly: the Mishnah was written in a world very different from today's, and its frame is a man's.
Third, the rabbis also built protections inside that frame, and you'll meet some this week: a contract that guards a wife, a ruling that weeps over divorce, a long struggle for women left stranded.
Jews today live with this order in different ways. Orthodox communities keep its law and work within it, for example with prenuptial agreements. Conservative rabbis have added clauses and rulings.
Reform and Reconstructionist Jews often reshape the ceremonies so both partners speak and give.
What they share is the order's deepest claim: a promise between two people is holy ground. The Talmud even compares a bride to something set apart for the Temple.

how: Jewish weddings, divorces and vows follow rules that grow out of this order; Orthodox communities apply them as halacha, Conservative rabbis apply them with their own rulings, and Reform and Reconstructionist couples often adapt the ceremonies so that both partners speak.

games.q: you made a vow out loud last month. now it's inconvenient, and no one remembers you said it. what does the Torah say?
o: it was only words; let it go.
do according to all that came out of your mouth.
make a new vow to replace it.
games.why: the verse on vows says he shall not break his word, and shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.

practice: Bring to mind one commitment you've made, a marriage, a friendship, a promise to a parent or a child, a vow to yourself, and remember the words, if there were words, and who heard them.
Then ask, without judging, how that promise is doing now. Look at it the way you'd look at something precious on a shelf.
